content.text: {"relation": "DIVERGENT", "consensus_summary": "All four blind responses converge on the garden as paradise: the place of God's presence and unbroken communion with humanity, framed by Eden lost (Genesis 2-3) and Eden restored (Revelation 21-22), with well-attested secondary readings (garden-as-temple, Song of Songs bride/soul/church, Gethsemane obedience-testing, watered-garden fruitfulness, garden-tomb new creation).", "book_summary": "The book defines the garden as a planted grouping of trees, where trees symbolize nations or peoples arranged together under a gardener's (ruler's) authority — an explicitly political/collective identification, citing Ezekiel 31:9 and cross-referencing its 'Trees' entry. It flags the paradise/Eden-fellowship reading as merely the common teaching.", "consensus_core_identification": "Garden = paradise, the sphere of God's presence and fellowship with humanity, lost in Eden and restored in the new creation.", "book_core_identification": "Garden = an arranged collection of nations/peoples (symbolized as trees) governed together under a gardener/ruler.", "core_relation": "CONTRADICTS", "extension_relation": "PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION", "boundary_disagreement": "The book reclassifies garden passages — including the 'garden of God' containing the trees of Eden (Ezek 31:9) — from images of paradise and divine communion into images of geopolitical arrangement: nations grouped under a sovereign. It does not merely narrow which gardens count; it changes what any garden signifies. Cases the consensus treats as sacred-space/fellowship imagery (Eden, garden of God) are recast as corporate-political imagery, while consensus cases like Gethsemane, the garden tomb, and the Song of Songs garden are simply unaddressed by the entry.", "material_contradiction": "The consensus says the garden signifies the place of God's presence and human fellowship with God (paradise); the book says it signifies an assembly of nations/peoples under a ruler's governance. These are different referents in the same contexts: a state of communion with God versus a collective of political entities. The book's own common-view note marks the paradise reading as the teaching it departs from, so accepting the book's identification requires rejecting the consensus core rather than refining its boundary.", "rationale": "Both axes point away from MATCH or REFINED. The book does not retain the consensus category (paradise/divine presence) and adjust its edges; it substitutes a wholly different symbolic decoding built on its trees-as-nations system. No blind response, including the minority alternatives (temple-sanctuary, bride/soul, literal geography, general fertility), anticipates a nations-under-a-ruler reading, but the book's claim is not merely absent from consensus — it directly displaces the central identification the consensus asserts for the same passages (Eden / garden of God). That is replacement of the referent, hence DIVERGENT rather than NOVEL or REFINED.", "citation_support": "PARTIAL", "strongest_objection": "Ezekiel 31 is genuinely a passage where trees represent nations (Assyria as a great cedar envied by 'the trees of Eden... in the garden of God'), so the book's single citation does support tree-as-nation symbolism in that context; a defender could argue the book is generalizing a real prophetic idiom, and that the consensus itself concedes 'garden' has multiple context-dependent referents (Response C denies settled consensus), which weakens the claim of a single contradicted core. However, one contextually apt citation cannot carry the definition across Genesis, the Song of Songs, the Gospels, and Revelation, where the paradise/presence reading dominates.", "confidence": "high"}
